title: Line of Sight Helper: Two-Point Visibility
description: Estimate line of sight between two points with the Line of Sight Helper — combined horizon ranges, endpoint elevations and curvature checks. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, two 30 m towers on flat ground can see each other's tops at 39.1 km — each contributes its own 19.6 km horizon, and the sight line just grazes the curve between them.
quick_answer: The Line of Sight Helper estimates geometric line of sight between two points: it combines both endpoints' horizon distances and compares their elevations for a rough visibility verdict. Enter the two heights and read whether the curve of the Earth alone permits the view.

CCTV, wildfire lookout cameras and wildlife monitors all ask the same question this page prices: what ground is mutually visible?
Two hilltops, two torches, one calculation — the helper is the worksheet version of the horizon's geometry.

Two 30 m towers: 19.6 + 19.6 = 39.1 km of combined range. Put them 45 km apart and the Earth's curve alone forbids the view — no mast paint or optimism changes it; taller towers or a relay are the only votes that count.
A 500 m hill (horizon 79.8 km) watching a harbour buoy (height ~3 m, horizon 6.2 km): range ≈ 86 km. One high endpoint does nearly all the work — height is the currency, and it is not shared equally.

popular_table.note: Ranges assume a smooth spherical Earth and clear air. Real paths add terrain, buildings, trees — and refraction, which typically stretches these figures by about 8%.

faq: What does 'rough' mean in the verdict?
The helper judges the planet's curve and the endpoints only. A ridge, a wood or a city between the points can block a geometrically open line — profile the path for the full answer.
Standard refraction lengthens both horizons (the 7⁄6-radius model), adding roughly 8% to ranges on a typical day. The helper's headline numbers stay geometric so the margin is yours to see.
Then its horizon is ~0 and the range is just the high end's horizon — a ship's masthead sighting a lighthouse works exactly this way, in reverse.
Heights above sea level or above ground?

What matters is height above the surface the sight line grazes — hilltop elevation plus structure height, in the terrain's own terms. A 30 m tower in a valley is not a 30 m advantage over the ridge next door.
Can I check a specific obstruction?
That is the Hidden Height and path-profile work: this helper sets the outer bound (can the endpoints see each other at all over the curve), profiles settle the middle.
A bright light can be detected slightly beyond the visual horizon by its glow and loom — the geometry of the lamp itself is unchanged, and this page prices the lamp, not the loom.
No — line of sight here is the surface geometry of light travelling straight. Sound, radio diffraction and seismic paths each bend by their own rules.

Summit-to-summit records run past 480 km in exceptional clarity (the famous Pyrenees–Alps photographs) — combined horizons of two high peaks plus generous refraction. The arithmetic scales; the air rarely cooperates.
